title: Office Politics, Played in Daylight
summary: Politics is what happens when facts alone can't settle a decision. How to read incentives, pre-align in the open, disagree and commit, and know when to walk away.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Your design doc is solid. The risks are written down, the estimate is honest, and the meeting still moves on in five minutes. Whatever sank it usually isn't in the doc. Sales already promised a date. Ops is still worn out from last month's incident. Another team is worried about losing ownership of the service. The person who signs off will take the blame if it breaks.

Welcome to office politics. The ugly versions are easy to spot: hoarding information, taking credit, private alliances, letting someone else take the fall. Most of it is more ordinary than that. Every company has limited attention, budget, authority and appetite for risk, and everyone holds a different piece of the truth. Politics is what happens when those differences shape a decision that facts alone can't settle. You can't opt out of that part. You can choose how you play it.

Map responsibilities, not motives

You don't need to sort colleagues into allies and enemies. A more useful map asks four things about each person: what they're responsible for, what failure would cost them, what they know that you don't, and what they can't approve on their own. The product lead pushing for speed may be protecting a promise to a big customer. The platform engineer asking for another week may still be cleaning up after a shaky release. Neither position tells you who they are as people. It tells you what their role makes them see.

Guessing what someone "really wants" breeds suspicion and gossip. Asking a question they can actually answer gets you facts you can check.

The guess The question
"She just wants the credit." "Which commitment is this date protecting?"
"They're stalling." "What would you need to see to feel OK shipping this week?"
"He blocks everything we propose." "What changed since we last talked about this?"
"Nobody here can decide anything." "Who makes the final call, and by when?"

Translate without bending the facts

Next comes translation. An engineering risk should arrive with consequences other people can weigh: how long we might be down, how many support tickets that means, whether the data can be recovered, what a rollback costs. Business urgency should come back to engineering as a stated constraint ("we promised this customer a demo on the 12th"), never as a vague "leadership wants it." Unknowns stay unknown. Translation only helps when the evidence survives the trip.

Michael Nygard's architecture decision records have a nice detail here. The Context section describes "the forces at play," and he lists "technological, political, social, and project local" forces side by side, in value-neutral language that simply states facts (Nygard, 2011). Politics belongs in the doc too, written as plainly as the latency numbers.

Pre-align in daylight

Talking with the people affected before the formal review is smart. Lean practitioners call it nemawashi: "gaining acceptance and preapproval for a proposal" by walking management and stakeholders through it first, "to get input, anticipate resistance" and fit the change with other priorities (Lean Enterprise Institute). They get time to find the gaps. You get time to fix them.

Pre-alignment turns sour when you tell each room a different story to collect votes. Share the same facts everywhere, ask for the hardest objection, and bring real concerns back into the shared doc. Here's a simple test: if something you said in private would be embarrassing to repeat in the meeting, it wasn't alignment.

Disagree cleanly, then commit

A clean disagreement has a shape. Say what worries you without diagnosing anyone's character. Show the evidence and where it runs out. Explain what happens if you're right, then offer an alternative or a condition that makes the original plan safer. Be clear about who owns the decision and when it's due.

Then let it go. Amazon writes this straight into its leadership principles: leaders "respectfully challenge decisions when they disagree," and "once a decision is determined, they commit wholly" (Amazon Leadership Principles). Reopening a settled decision through slow-walking and side comments is the classic political move, and teams spot it fast. The exceptions are serious ones: lying, anything illegal, real harm to users or colleagues. Those never get dressed up as alignment.

Write it down, share the credit

A short recap keeps everyone honest: what we decided, why, who owns it, what risk is left, and when we'll check again. Nobody should be saving it up for a future "told you so." It gives the team a memory that doesn't shift with whoever is most senior or most confident in the room.

Visibility works the same way. Work nobody can find is hard to learn from, support or reward fairly. A useful update names the outcome, the people who helped, the risk you reduced and what's still unfinished. No need to turn normal work into a hero story. Leave enough of a trail that the next decision rests on facts, so the loudest voice doesn't get to write the whole history.

Know where your line is

Being politically aware never requires leaking confidential information, flattering whoever has power, hiding a risk, ganging up on a colleague or taking credit that belongs to someone else. When things get slippery, go back to moves that hold up in daylight: ask directly, record the decision, include the people affected, fix a wrong attribution, and refuse to say something you know is false. You can stay friendly and still say no.

When the room isn't worth it

Sometimes you do all of this and nothing improves. One bad meeting doesn't prove a workplace is broken. A pattern is different: people who flag risks get punished, decisions get rewritten after the fact, credit keeps flowing to the same few people, setting a boundary brings retaliation, ethics concerns have no safe path upward. Write down what happened, with dates, and take it to your manager, a senior you trust or the right internal channel. That usually shows you whether repair is possible. If the place keeps asking you to stay silent or act against what you believe, leaving is a reasonable boundary, and nobody gets to call it losing.

Try this week

  • Pick one person you keep clashing with and write down what they're responsible for and what failure would cost them.
  • Turn one motive guess into a question from the table above, and ask it.
  • Before your next review, send the same draft to everyone affected and ask for the hardest objection.
  • After the next decision, post a five-line recap: decision, reason, owner, remaining risk, next check.

A lot of politics grows out of vague communication. If that sounds familiar, Signals or Messages covers that side of the story.

faqs.a: No. The ugly parts (hoarding information, taking credit, private alliances) are real, but most politics comes from limited budget, attention and authority, plus people holding different pieces of the truth. It shows up whenever facts alone can't settle a decision. You can take part honestly by sharing context and keeping decisions visible.

faqs.q: How do I figure out what's driving someone's position?
faqs.a: Look at their responsibilities instead of guessing motives. Ask what they own, what failure would cost them, what they know that you don't, and what they can't approve alone. Then ask checkable questions, such as which commitment a date protects or who makes the final call and by when.

faqs.q: Is talking to stakeholders before a meeting manipulative?
faqs.a: Not when it's done openly. Lean teams call it nemawashi: walking stakeholders through a proposal early to get input and anticipate resistance. It goes wrong when you tell each person a different story to collect votes. Share the same facts with everyone and bring real concerns back into the shared document.

faqs.q: What should I do after losing a disagreement?
faqs.a: Commit to the decision. Amazon's leadership principles ask people to challenge decisions respectfully and then commit wholly once a decision is made. Reopening it through delay or side comments erodes trust. The exceptions are deception, illegal conduct or real harm, which should be raised through proper channels.

faqs.q: When is it time to leave a political workplace?
faqs.a: One bad meeting isn't enough. A repeated pattern is: people punished for flagging risks, decisions rewritten afterward, credit regularly taken, retaliation for boundaries, no safe way to raise ethics concerns. Document it and seek help through a manager, a trusted senior or an internal channel. If nothing changes, leaving is a reasonable boundary.
